description: We are AVIRA_LunarNav_RELOADED, an innovation-driven team participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Led by a software engineer from India with 13+ years of experience in C/C++, embedded systems, algorithms and system architecture, we aim to develop a data-driven Lunar Landing Site Navigator using NASA datasets, AI, 3D visualization and scientific analysis. We welcome global collaborators skilled in astronomy, lunar science, Python, AI/ML, 3D graphics and UI/UX.
summary:
**The Moon doesn't wait. Neither should mission decisions.**

A lunar south-pole landing site may look promising—until a mission delay changes its sunlight, Earth visibility, communication windows or power constraints. Finding a location is only the beginning. Understanding whether the mission scenario still meets its requirements is the real challenge.

**AVIRA LunarNav RELOADED** is a working Python/Streamlit prototype that compares lunar landing sites and dates, visualizes sampled Sun/Earth positions relative to the local horizon, and evaluates illumination, direct-to-Earth visibility, communication blackouts and simplified battery reserves.

**Our USP: INPUT → DETECT → EXPLAIN → RECOVER → VERIFY.** Rather than merely ranking locations, AVIRA identifies constraint failures, explains the supporting measurements and enables exploration of alternative sites, dates and fault scenarios.

**Our evidence:** 49 automated tests passed. In a 120-hour demonstration, Candidate A achieved 62 hours of joint visibility versus 54 hours for Candidate B. Yet neither met all configured constraints.

With a NASA/JPL Horizons integration pathway, interactive visualization and reproducible outputs, AVIRA aims to make early-stage lunar mission screening understandable, transparent and evidence-driven.
details:
AVIRA LunarNav RELOADED

The Moon Doesn't Wait. Neither Should Mission Decisions.

Don't just find a landing site. Understand the mission.

1. THE PROBLEM — A Promising Site Can Still Fail

Imagine a lunar mission preparing to land near the Moon's south pole.

A landing site has been selected. Its location looks promising.

Then the landing date changes.

The relative positions of the Sun and Earth change. Expected illumination and communication windows may no longer support the mission's operating assumptions.

Mission planners must answer five critical questions:

  1. How long will the Sun be geometrically visible?
  2. When can Earth be seen above the lunar horizon for direct-to-Earth communication?
  3. How long could communication blackouts last?
  4. Do power and battery assumptions satisfy configured requirements?
  5. Could a different landing site or mission date offer better conditions?

Our problem statement: Finding a landing site is not enough. Mission planners must understand which constraints are satisfied, which fail, and what alternatives deserve investigation.

2. OUR SOLUTION — From Lunar Geometry to Mission Decisions

We developed AVIRA LunarNav RELOADED, a working Python/Streamlit lunar mission-window screening application.

The application brings together:

  • Candidate landing-site and mission-date comparisons.
  • Sampled Sun/Earth elevation and local-horizon visibility.
  • Sunlight and direct-to-Earth geometric visibility windows.
  • Communication-blackout duration analysis.
  • Simplified solar-energy and battery-reserve estimates.
  • Configurable engineering constraints.
  • Alternative-site, alternative-date and fault-injection scenarios.
  • Interactive charts and conceptual 3D geometry.
  • Test evidence, reproducibility information and source disclosures.

AVIRA does more than display lunar conditions: it explains when a scenario fails its configured requirements.

3. OUR USP — Detect. Explain. Recover. Verify.

A location that performs better than another may still fail mission constraints.

Our five-stage workflow is:

INPUT — Define the Mission: Select coordinates, UTC dates, evaluation period, assumptions and screening thresholds.

DETECT — Identify the Risk: Calculate sampled illumination and Earth-visibility windows, blackout durations and simplified power conditions.

EXPLAIN — Understand the Failure: Display supporting measurements and highlight constraint violations using PASS, FAIL or UNKNOWN outcomes.

RECOVER — Investigate Alternatives: Compare another site, a different date or modified scenario assumptions.

VERIFY — Review Evidence: Inspect charts, assumptions, data sources, reproducible results and automated tests.

Our USP: The integration of lunar geometry, constraint-failure explanation, alternative exploration and evidence-aware screening in one workflow.

We do not claim to invent lunar ephemerides, scientific mapping or site-ranking technology.

4. THE PROOF — The Better Site Was Still Not Good Enough

This is a functioning software prototype, not just a concept.

The application was executed locally on Windows using Python 3.12 and Streamlit.

Automated software verification: 49 tests passed, zero failed.

An illustrative 120-hour scenario compared two lunar south-pole candidate sites.

The Critical Engineering Finding

Candidate A provides eight more sampled hours of joint visibility than Candidate B.

At first glance, Candidate A appears preferable.

But both candidates fail the configured overall constraints.

AVIRA reports those failures instead of presenting the higher-ranked candidate as safe.

Better doesn't mean feasible.

This demonstrates the difference between relative performance and constraint satisfaction.

These are observed prototype outputs, not independently validated NASA mission measurements.

5. HOW WE BUILT IT — Working Software and Test Evidence

Application and Interface

  • Python 3.12 and Streamlit.
  • Configurable scenario inputs and interactive results.
  • CSV and reproducibility exports.

NASA Data and Geometry

  • NASA/JPL Horizons API integration pathway for Sun/Earth observer ephemerides.
  • Sampled geometric visibility and elevation calculations.
  • Offline synthetic demonstration mode.

Engineering Screening

  • Joint Sun/Earth visibility analysis.
  • Communication-blackout calculations.
  • Simplified battery and power-reserve estimation.
  • Configurable thresholds and PASS / FAIL / UNKNOWN outcomes.
  • Site/date what-if analysis and fault injection.

Visualization and Software Quality

  • Interactive engineering graphs.
  • Conceptual procedural 3D observation geometry.
  • Actual application screenshots.
  • 49 passing automated Python tests.

6. INTENDED IMPACT — Why It Matters

Mission-concept teams: Investigate site/date trade-offs before higher-fidelity planning.

Engineers and researchers: Understand how multiple constraints interact rather than relying on one score.

Educators and students: Explore lunar geometry, sunlight, communication blackouts and simplified energy planning.

The public: Understand why landing-site selection is more complex than choosing coordinates on a map.

Our intended impact: Make early-stage lunar mission screening more understandable, reproducible and evidence-driven.

7. SCIENTIFIC RESPONSIBILITY — What We Know and What Remains

The application implements established geometric concepts and includes a NASA/JPL Horizons live-data integration pathway.

Current limitations include:

  • Raw Horizons outputs have not yet been independently cross-validated against preserved source responses.
  • Validated site-specific lunar terrain and horizon blocking are not integrated.
  • Geometric sunlight visibility does not prove usable electrical power.
  • Earth visibility alone does not guarantee a functioning communication link.
  • Battery calculations use simplified assumptions.
  • Synthetic outputs are not certified NASA observations.
  • Conceptual 3D imagery is not validated lunar terrain.

AVIRA is a research and educational prototype—not flight-qualified landing-safety software.

8. FUTURE DEVELOPMENT — Toward Higher-Fidelity Screening

Our planned improvements include:

  1. Integrating validated lunar terrain and horizon data.
  2. Independently validating NASA/JPL Horizons calculations.
  3. Improving solar-power and battery-reserve modeling.
  4. Introducing realistic communication-link and mission-operation constraints.
  5. Expanding multi-site and multi-date scenario analysis.
  6. Strengthening data provenance and scientific verification.

9. FINAL MESSAGE — From Lunar Data to Mission Decisions

A landing site can look better and still fail.

AVIRA LunarNav RELOADED makes that distinction visible.

Instead of asking only:

“Which landing site looks best?”

We ask:

“Which mission requirements are satisfied? What failed? Why did it fail? And what alternatives should we investigate next?”

AVIRA LunarNav RELOADED

Explore the Moon. Explain the Risk. Investigate the Next Move.
